stances.claim: The election of Archbishop Socrates B. Villegas to the CBCP presidency complements the renewal of the Catholic Church in our country that began with the elevation of Archbishop Luis Antonio G. Tagle to the College of Cardinals. Both are young, humble, prayerful, and empowering. In a larger sense, these two shepherds echo the simplicity and theology of reformist Pope Francis in the universal Church -- great communicators in the new media (straightforward, uncomplicated, direct from the heart); they unravel the great mysteries of Christianity and the ponderous papal encyclicals via their plain, everyday language and their simple, austere lifestyle.

Newly elevated they may all have been and newly minted their messages may appear to be, in my humble view they really bring back the Church to its roots -- to the original rock the Lord Jesus Christ founded and anchored it -- a Church of the poor, by the poor, and for the poor. PCP II (Jan 20-Feb 17 1991, implementing Vatican II 1962-65) defined it as 'A Church that embraces and practices the evangelical spirit of poverty which combines detachment from possessions with a profound trust in the Lord as the only source of salvation... A Church that will courageously defend and vindicate the rights of the poor and the oppressed even when doing so will mean alienation or persecution from the rich and powerful... A Church where nobody is so poor as to have nothing to give, and nobody so rich as to have nothing to receive.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Church-of-the-poor PCP II verbatim-citation definitional anchor

stances.claim: The new leaders are steering the Church back to Jesus Christ who identified Himself with the poor (Mt 25:40,45). By reaching out to the poor and liberating them from their misery, the new shepherds echo Jesus's mission (Lk 4:18 'The spirit of the Lord is upon me. He has anointed me to bring good news to the poor'). When Pope Francis forsook his gilded seat, I was reminded that Jesus's throne was a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven through His palm. Jesus made it absolutely clear who He was, what His objectives were, and how He intended to accomplish them.

Jesus explained in different ways to different people. To His disciples, He taught loftily, authoritatively -- in His Sermon on the Mount He leaned in favor of the poor, sorrowing, simple-hearted, peacemakers, and condemned the hypocrite, arrogant, proud, self-righteous; He forgave the repentant and simple-hearted. To the nondisciples, He spoke in parables intended 'to enable the listener to discover something for himself' -- awakening faith and making the nonbeliever discover the truth without being lectured on. Most parables ended with questions ('Which of these three, do you think, made himself neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?' -- good Samaritan, Lk 10:36; 'Now, what will the owner of the vineyard do to them?' -- tenants, Lk 20:16).

Jesus was a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction. 2,000 years ago there was no freedom of speech, dissent, or opposition -- group conformity was the standard of truth and virtue. But Jesus was 'a man who had the courage of his convictions. No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed' (Albert Nolan, 'Jesus Before Christianity'). Jesus was a servant-leader who led by example (Mk 10:42-45 -- 'the so-called rulers of the nation act as tyrants and their great ones oppress them. But it shall not be so among you; whoever would be great among you must be your servant'); to show readiness to perform the humblest of service, He washed the feet of His apostles (Jn 13:13-14).

Jesus was a leader of intense prayer and unbending faith. The Bible is replete with stories of Jesus praying. In the Garden of Gethsemane, He prayed so intensely that 'great drops of blood formed like sweat and fell to the ground' (Lk 22:44). The renewal of the Church is an ever-continuing process and does not necessarily denigrate the old order -- in the same manner, parents are not diminished when their children surpass them. Congratulations to His Excellency, His Eminence, and His Holiness for renewing the Church and bringing it back to Jesus Christ.

notable_anecdotes: Pope Francis 'forsook his gilded seat' detail -- a concrete papal-simplicity image that triggers CJP's expansive Christological-poetics (Jesus's throne = wooden cross + crown = bouquet of thorns + scepter = lowly reed + ring = rusty nail through palm), among the most lyrical passages in this column.
PCP II verbatim-citation Church-of-the-poor definition -- among the longest verbatim doctrinal-document quotations in CJP's corpus, anchoring the entire column in 1991 conciliar authority.
The 'nobody so poor as to have nothing to give, and nobody so rich as to have nothing to receive' PCP II reciprocal-poverty formulation -- a memorable mutual-exchange aphorism captured verbatim.

The 'no freedom of speech, no freedom to dissent, no freedom to oppose. Group conformity was the standard of truth and virtue' 2,000-years-ago context -- CJP applying his free-expression columnist-perspective to Jesus's historical setting.

The Albert Nolan 'Jesus Before Christianity' citation -- 'No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed' -- among the rare extra-scriptural book-quotations in a CJP religious-theme column.

The parents-not-diminished-when-children-surpass-them closing analogy -- CJP's gentle formulation that the Church's renewal does not denigrate the old order, characteristic of his integrative-not-rejectionist approach.

The triple-honor closing 'Congratulations to His Excellency, His Eminence and His Holiness' -- addressing Villegas/Tagle/Francis in their respective formal ecclesial titles, an unusually formal three-tier salutation register.

The 'great drops of blood formed like sweat and fell to the ground' (Lk 22:44) Gethsemane prayer-intensity citation -- a vividly physical scriptural image deployed to anchor Jesus-as-intense-prayer characterization.

The parables-ending-with-questions analysis -- citing both Lk 10:36 (good Samaritan) and Lk 20:16 (tenants) -- captures Jesus's pedagogy as discovery-prompting rather than lecture-delivering, a methodological observation that doubles as a CJP self-reflective register on teaching.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames the election of Archbishop Socrates B. Villegas to the presidency of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines as the latest chapter in the renewal of the Catholic Church in the Philippines that began with Archbishop Luis Antonio G. Tagle's elevation to the College of Cardinals. Both are young, humble, prayerful, and empowering -- echoing the simplicity and theology of reformist Pope Francis in the universal Church: great communicators in new media, straightforward and uncomplicated, direct from the heart; they unravel the great mysteries of Christianity and the ponderous papal encyclicals via plain everyday language and their simple, austere lifestyle. Newly elevated though they may be and newly minted though their messages may appear, in CJP's humble view they really bring the Church back to its roots -- to the original rock the Lord Jesus Christ founded and anchored it: a Church of the poor, by the poor, and for the poor. He quotes the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (PCP II, Jan 20-Feb 17 1991, implementing Vatican II 1962-65): 'A Church that embraces and practices the evangelical spirit of poverty which combines detachment from possessions with a profound trust in the Lord as the only source of salvation... A Church that will courageously defend and vindicate the rights of the poor and the oppressed even when doing so will mean alienation or persecution from the rich and powerful... A Church where nobody is so poor as to have nothing to give, and nobody so rich as to have nothing to receive.' The new leaders are steering the Church back to Jesus Christ, who identified Himself with the poor (Mt 25:40,45). By reaching out to the poor and liberating them, they echo Jesus's mission (Lk 4:18). When Pope Francis forsook his gilded seat, CJP was reminded that Jesus's throne was a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven through His palm. Jesus explained in different ways: to His disciples, loftily and authoritatively (in His Sermon on the Mount favoring the poor, sorrowing, simple-hearted, peacemakers; condemning the hypocrite, arrogant, proud, self-righteous); to nondisciples in parables ending with questions -- Lk 10:36 (the good Samaritan: 'Which of these three, do you think, made himself neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?') and Lk 20:16 (the tenants: 'Now, what will the owner of the vineyard do to them?') -- awakening faith and making the nonbeliever discover the truth without being lectured on. Jesus was a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction: 2,000 years ago there was no freedom of speech, dissent, or opposition -- group conformity was the standard of truth and virtue -- but, in Albert Nolan's words ('Jesus Before Christianity'), 'No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed.' Jesus was a servant-leader who led by example (Mk 10:42-45 -- 'whoever would be great among you must be your servant'); to show readiness to perform the humblest service, He washed the feet of His apostles (Jn 13:13-14). And He was a leader of intense prayer and unbending faith -- at Gethsemane, He prayed so intensely that 'great drops of blood formed like sweat and fell to the ground' (Lk 22:44). The renewal of the Church is an ever-continuing process and does not necessarily denigrate the old order -- parents are not diminished when their children surpass them. Congratulations to His Excellency, His Eminence, and His Holiness for renewing the Church and bringing it back to Jesus Christ.
